extracted.intended_audience: users of Isabelle/HOL learning the Isar structured proof language (readers familiar with natural deduction and Isabelle/HOL basics)
extracted.subtask_description: Authoring readable, maintainable structured proofs in the Isar proof language for Isabelle/HOL, using Isar constructs (proof/qed, assume/have/show, from/then/thus, cases, induction, obtain, etc.) and appropriate proof methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer structured Isar proofs for readability and maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Structured proofs are immensely more readable and maintainable than apply -scripts; Isar is a stylised language of mathematics whose proofs are readable for both human and machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Isar structure rather than long apply-scripts for communication/maintenance. If you don't yet know the structure, exploratory apply steps are acceptable initially, but convert to Isar top-down once the structure is understood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the proof ... qed / by method skeleton correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof can be either compound (proof – qed) or atomic (by method). show establishes the conclusion of the theorem; intermediate have statements do not contribute to the theorem's top-level statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use assume/have/show in the expected roles; comments begin with “—”. Use 'by method' for short atomic steps and 'proof' ... 'qed' for structured proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the proof command auto-select introduction rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Command proof automatically tries to select an introduction rule based on the goal and a predefined list of rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit explicit rule application when an introduction rule matches the goal; rely on default selection to simplify proof text (e.g., impI applied automatically).

rubrics_metrics.name: Feed facts into proofs (UNIX-like pipe model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange the sequence of propositions in a UNIX-like pipe so the proof of each proposition builds on the previous proposition; use from fact show ... proof to pipe facts into the next step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer piping (from/then/this/thus) to naming; this reduces clutter and clarifies forward reasoning. Example abbreviations: then = from this, thus = then show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use then/this/thus abbreviations to avoid naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'this' to refer to the previous proposition and abbreviations then = from this and thus = then show to streamline references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These abbreviations reduce explicit naming and keep proofs linear and readable; prefer them when earlier propositions are the obvious inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate multiple subgoals with next
rubrics_metrics.description: next deals with multiple subgoals: each subgoal is proved separately and proofs are separated with next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use next between subproofs when showing conjunctive or multiple-goal conclusions; next is strictly required when subgoals are in different assumption contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid duplication by using patterns (is ...) and assumes/shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Use (is "pattern") to pattern-match large formulae and name parts with ?-variables; use assumes and shows elements to name assumptions and conclusions directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern matching prevents repeating large expressions; assumes/ shows give direct names for assumptions and the goal, simplifying later references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use using to add facts before a proof to trigger eliminations
rubrics_metrics.description: Command using can appear before a proof and adds further facts to those piped into the proof, which may trigger elimination rules implicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place 'using ab' before proof to feed ab into the proof and cause appropriate elimination rules to be applied automatically, avoiding repeated manual elimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppress implicit rule application with '-' when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple '-' prevents implicit selection of introduction/elimination rules that might perform unintended decompositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin a proof with proof - or show P - to avoid Isar implicitly applying introduction/elimination rules (e.g., to avoid an unwanted ∨-introduction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer quoting facts by content or using assms over unnecessary naming
rubrics_metrics.description: You can refer to a fact by its content using back quotes (e.g., `A ∨ B`) or use assms to refer to the list of assumptions; use indexing like assms(2) to pick specific assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting is best for small formulae and immediately reveals the fact to the reader; avoid introducing names unless necessary for clarity or multiple uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple facts with moreover / ultimately instead of many names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use moreover between fact proofs to form a sequence and ultimately to combine them into from A1 ... An.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This idiom avoids naming each fact when you need to feed several facts together into a subsequent step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fix/show for universal quantifiers (introducing local variables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Command fix introduces new local variables in the proof; fix/show corresponds to the universal quantifier at the meta-level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fix a before proving statements about an arbitrary a; choose local names freely since they are irrelevant outside the block.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer obtain over explicit ∃-elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: obtain provides a more appealing form of generalized existence reasoning and mirrors usual mathematical style when working from ∃x. P(x) to P(x) with a new local variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'from Pf obtain x where "P(f x)" ..' rather than writing exE with fix/assume; obtain packages the necessary variable introduction and soundness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use automatic proof methods (simp, blast, contradiction, best) appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful automatic methods can be used for bigger proof steps; e.g. blast for predicate calculus reasoning, simp for simplification, contradiction if P and ¬P are available, and best for best-first search.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer using automatic methods to shorten proofs but be mindful of readability: very terse blast steps may be cryptic—provide a more detailed version if necessary. Use 'by best' to let search find the proof when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use let to introduce abbreviations for complex terms
rubrics_metrics.description: let introduces an abbreviation for a term (e.g., let ?S = "{x. x ∉ f x}").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Name complex witnesses and repeated terms with let to improve readability and avoid repeating the same expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use raw proof blocks ({ ... }) and have for emergent lemmas to avoid duplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Raw proof blocks yield conclusions from their fixes/assumes/have without stating an explicit property; they are useful to avoid step-by-step decomposition and duplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enclose local derivations in { ... } and follow with 'thus' or 'note' to use the emergent result; prefer stating the desired form and letting methods verify it rather than manipulating proof state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not manipulate the proof state; state the desired form instead
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not apply proof methods to transform the proof state into a particular form; state the desired form explicitly and let proof methods verify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This yields more readable and robust proofs. Use have/obtain/raw blocks to express intermediate claims rather than forcing state changes with sequences of rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perform case distinctions with cases/case and be aware of subgoal ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proof (cases ...) or proof cases; the order of cases can matter because cases abbreviates (rule case_split) and may instantiate ?P in unintended ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When A is large, use proof (cases "A") or named case patterns (case True/False) to avoid repeating A and to allow arbitrary order of proving cases; use case (Constructor vars) to name variables introduced by the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use induct / induction idioms: name cases, use arbitrary for generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: For structural induction use proof (induct n) or proof (induct xs arbitrary: vars) and case (Suc i) / case 0 to name and access local variables and induction hypotheses; arbitrary universally quantifies vars before induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a proof needs generalization for induction, pass arbitrary: vars so the induction hypothesis becomes applicable. Use case (Constructor vars) to bind anonymous variables for reference in the step case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use rule induction for inductively defined sets mirroring the defining rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule induction is triggered by piping a fact (x1,...,xn) ∈ R into the proof and produces one case per defining rule with the same names, following the inductive definition closely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feed the relevant assumptions via using/assms; expect one case per constructor/rule and use the induction hypothesis (IH) appropriately (e.g., IH[OF ...]) for forward reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name and recall intermediate facts with note
rubrics_metrics.description: Use note to remember intermediate facts that cannot be named directly; note some_name = this gives the result of a raw block a name and sets this to the list of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use note for capturing emergent facts from raw blocks or to recall existing named facts in more convenient forms (note some_fact).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fixes to declare type constraints and local concrete syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: fixes allows decorating propositions with type constraints and introducing concrete syntax locally so that the theorem statement is clearer and local names are available in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer fixes f :: 'a => 'a set instead of putting type constraints in the quoted theorem text; fixes also supports specifying infix notation locally and removes it after the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use obtain to introduce multiple witnesses and propositions succinctly
rubrics_metrics.description: obtain can introduce multiple witnesses and their associated propositions in one statement (e.g., from A obtain x y where P: "P x y" and Q: "Q x y" by blast).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is more convenient than explicit exE eliminations and keeps proofs closer to customary mathematical presentations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sorry only in quick-and-dirty mode for top-down development
rubrics_metrics.description: Command sorry proves anything but is only allowed in quick and dirty mode; it is convenient for sketching proofs or top-down development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not leave sorry in final developments; use it only during exploratory or incremental proof construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine proof styles sparingly; avoid leaving large apply-scripts inside Isar leaves
rubrics_metrics.description: While whole apply-scripts may appear in leaves of an Isar proof, this is best avoided; when converting apply-style proofs to Isar you can proceed top-down and leave small scripts at leaves if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer expressing outer structure in Isar and keep leaves minimal; resort to apply-style only when automatic steps or Isar constructs cannot achieve the desired goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of implicit elimination/introduction priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Isar's default behavior is to try elimination rules first when there are incoming facts (.. is short for by(rule elim-rules intro-rules)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember eliminations have priority over introductions and arrange incoming facts (order matters) or suppress implicit behavior (using '-') to avoid unintended rule application.
